list.listitem: Acute otitis externa is of bacterial origin in 90% or more of cases and fungal in 2-10%. Chronic otitis externa, unless the result of inadequately treated acute disease, commonly originates from a local allergic response or a systemic dermatitis.
Patients typically present with rapid onset of otalgia and signs of ear canal inflammation. C
Topical therapy () is adequate for the preponderance of otitis externa, reserving adjunctive oral therapy for severe disease or moderate disease in the immunocompromised. A
Pain should be assessed and analgesic treatment used as warranted. C
Preventive measures, from avoiding self-instrumentation of the auditory canal to removing water from the canal after swimming, may diminish recurence of disease but are unproven. C

background.definition: Otitis externa (also called "swimmers' ear") is a cellulitis of the ear canal skin with variable amounts of edema.

list.listitem: Cited as 0.4% to 1% per year, per the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 8.1 per 1000 population in the United States, higher in summer months and among children 5 to 14 years of age.
Lifetime incidence of 10%.

A British study found a rapid increase in the incidence of necrotizing otitis externa in England from 2002 to 2017. They hypothesis that it may be due to increasing prevalence of diabetes, increasing physician awareness, antibiotic resistance, and an aging population.
Bacteria are the cause of 90% or more of acute otitis externa.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa (20%-60%) and Staphylococcus aureus (10%-70%) are the most common bacterial organisms in acute otitis externa .
Fungal causes are unusual except in chronic otitis externa, following topical antibiotic treatment or in the immunosuppressed, and are usually Aspergillus or Candida.

Contact dermatitis (e.g., metal in earrings, cosmetics, hearing aids, agent in ear drops such as neomycin) or the ear canal manifestations of a systemic dermatitis (e.g., eczema, psoriasis) cause the preponderance of chronic otitis externa.
Excessive moisture from sweat or water (e.g., from swimming, trapped by cerumen or plugs) promote growth of canal microorganisms and canal skin maceration.
Disruption of cerumen barrier or canal skin (e.g., instrumentation with cotton swab, maceration from excessive moisture) promote growth and access of canal microorganisms.
Canal pH 7.0 or greater promotes overgrowth of microorganisms .

Preventive measures are largely unstudied and recommended based on expert opinion. They include removing obstructing cerumen, using ear plugs while swimming and then a hair dryer to dry the canal, and avoiding instrumentation. C
Swimming near the surface without ear plugs is safe in children with tympanostomy tubes. B
Acidifying ear drops before and after swimming and at bedtime have also been recommended. C
Patients typically present with rapid onset of otalgia. C
Signs and symptoms of ear canal inflammation are also present. C

Differential.Differential_Features: time course of <3 months, tympanic membrane bulging, no canal inflammation
time course of 3 or more months, middle ear effusion, no canal inflammation
cutaneous manifestations of systemic disease (e.g., eczema, psoriasis), some of which affects an ear canal
time course of <3 months, extracanal manifestations of disease spread, and/or temporal bone osteomyelitis

list.listitem: See for formal diagnostic criteria.
Patients usually present with a history of rapid onset of ear pain, usually within 48 hours. Otalgia may be severe; patients may also describe itching or a feeling of fullness.

On examination, there is usually tenderness of the tragus, pinna, or both and pain with movement of the pinna. Otoscopy may reveal diffuse ear canal edema, erythema, or both. It may also reveal maceration and inflammation of the ear canal and accumulated canal secretions
Look for any evidence of extracanal spread such as to the auricle or parotid or cervical nodes.
See for formal diagnostic criteria.

Topical anesthetic cream has been used to provide enough analgesia to facilitate cleaning of the canal but has not been studied, and presents the challenge of application through whatever debris or cerumen warrants the cleaning.
Use otoscopy (including pneumatic) to examine the patient, especially if integrity of the tympanic membrane or presence of fluid in the middle ear is in question.

Consider culture of canal secretions if there are extracanal manifestations of disease, to guide selection of oral or intravenous antibiotic, or if initial therapy fails and there is need to establish whether bacteria or fungi are involved and, if bacteria, of which type (e.g., Staph aureus vs. Pseudomonas aeruginosa).

Order a CT scan of temporal bone if extracanal manifestions and level of pain indicate severe disease, or if the patient is dizzy (8th cranial nerve) or has an ipsilateral facial weakness (7th cranial nerve).
Diagnosis is based on physical findings and history in the preponderance of patients.
As outlined under Diagnostic Tests, culture is occasionally necessary to differentiate bacterial from fungal infections in patients who do not respond to the initial choice of topical therapy.
For patients with severe symptoms, consider CT of temporal bone.
Treat pain with appropriate (usually oral) analgesia. A

Topical treatment () should be the first choice in uncomplicated cases. Treatment usually involves an acidifying agent for mild disease, escalating to an antibiotic, with or without a corticosteroid, as increased symptoms/signs warrant. A
Neomycin-containing products should not be used in patients with a perforated eardrum. C
A wick is not recommended except if the ear canal is sufficiently edematous that eardrop penetration to the medial canal is not assured. C

Follow-up reassessment should occur if significant symptom improvement does not occur within 48 to 72 hours. Assess for adequate use of previously prescribed treatment and for signs of disease extension to the auricle or nodes of the parotid or upper neck. C
IV antibiotics for a prolonged duration are recommended for necrotizing otitis externa. C

Pain, which can be severe, should be assessed and treated. Oral analgesics are preferred. Adding topical steroid to antibiotic treatment my hasten pain resolution.Topical benzocaine is often used but has not been studied for effectiveness. A randomized trial found that glycerol drops with 2% lidocaine were effective and safe for pain relief.

Topical treatment with an acidyfing agent or antibiotic, with or without a corticosteroid (), should be the first choice in uncomplicated cases. Acetic acid, boric acid, aluminum acetate, topical steroids alone or with acetic acid, and silver nitrate topical products are all effective.
All antibiotics produce similar results, resulting in clinical cure in 65% to 80% of patients within 10 days. There was no difference between quinolone and non-quinolone antibiotics.
Neomycin-containing products, including the suspension form, should not be used in patients with a perforated eardrum.

Up to 5% of individual can develop a hypersensitivity to topical neomycin and the resulting contact dermatitis can confuse the clinical picture, i.e., is failure of canal changes to improve due to resistance to the treatment or to the emerging manifestations of contact dermatitis.
Oral antibiotic are recommended for severe disease and for moderate disease in the immunocompromised.
Consider a topical steroid for allergic disease (e.g., contact sensitivity) or systemic dermatitis responsive to steroids.

The evidence supporting the use of a wick is not clear, and a wick is not recommended except if the ear canal is sufficiently edematous that the eardrops of choice can not penetrate to the medial canal.Ribbon gauze and ear wick are equally efficacious as packing materials in severe otitis media.
Warming of solutions to body temperature before irrigation decreases dizziness and reduces discomfort.
Low quality research shows little difference in outcomes among common treatment for otitis externa.

This severe infection is characterized by severe otalgia, purulent otorrhea, granulation tissue, spread of infection beyong the ear canal, and sometimes cranial nerve palsy. Most patients have diabetes, previous ear surgery, or immunosuppression.
The most common pathogen is Pseudomonas aeruginosa, with Staph aureus also commonly detected.
NHS Lothian guidelines recommend piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 gm IV once daily pending imaging confirmation for 2 weeks followed by 4 weeks of oral antibiotics.
Evidence is limited on the optimal treatment for necrotizing otitis externa. First-line therapy is most commonly inpatient, with an IV fluoroquinolone.
Clear obstructing debris or cerumen. Warmed solution is more comfortable for patients.
Institute culture directed intravenous antibiotics, and consider otolaryngology consultation for canal debridement which can include both necrotic skin and the underlying bone.
The 1:1 combination of isopropyl alcohol and white vinegar has not been formally studied for treatment or prevention but is similar in composition to commercially available products.
Tea tree oil has not been studied in the treatment of otitis externa, but in vitro research has shown 71% of Pseudomonas aeruginosa cultured from patients with acute otitis externa to be resistant.
Ear candling has been shown to be harmful.
Naturopathic herbal extract drops are as effective as anesthetic drops for children with otalgia.
Hyperbaric oxygen has been recommended for malignant otitis externa but a systematic review identified no clinical trials.
Analgesia for several days may be necessary, keeping in mind that such, particularly if topical, can mask failure of treatment.
Antibiotic/antiseptic treatment for 7 to 10 days.
Consider referral for extracanal manifestations of disease such as auricular cellulitis, parotitis, or cervical adenopathy in patients not responding to initial therapy.
Consider referral if patient has extracanal manifestations and is immunocompromised.
Refer if patient has facial weakness, vertigo, severe loss of auditory acuity, and/or temperature >39°C.
Prognosis is excellent for mild and moderate disease; it is guarded for severe disease in the immunocompromised, those who have had local irradiation, and the very elderly.
Follow-up reassessment should occur if significant symptom improvement does not occur within 72 hours. Assess for adequate use of previously prescribed treatment. C
Except in mild cases, patients should not swim for 7 to 10 days after treatment is started.
If possible, drops should be placed into the ear by someone else (especially if the patient is a child or elderly), because under-dosing has been reported with self-administration.

To use drops, the patient should be lying down with the affected ear facing upward. Enough drops should be used to fill the ear canal. The earlobe may need to be moved back and forth to remove air bubbles. The patient should remain in this position for 3 to 5 minutes and then let the solution drain. A cotton ball placed in the external os (canal opening) and adjacent conchal bowl of the auricle for a minute after assuming an upright position will absorp the excess eardrop solution that exits the canal and prevent such from wetting the patient's neck or shirt. The ear canal should be left open to dry.

feature.caption: Diagnostic Criteria for Acute Otitis Externa, From the American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Foundation.
feature.feature_body:
Rapid onset (generally within 48 h) in the past 3 weeks, AND Symptoms of ear canal inflammation that include: otalgia (often severe), itching, or fullness with or without hearing loss or pain in the ear canal with movement of the jaw AND
Signs of ear canal inflammation that include: tenderness of the tragus, pinna, or both OR diffuse ear canal edema, erythema, or both with or without otorrhea, regional lymphadenitis, tympanic membrane erythema, or cellulitis of the pinna and adjacent skin
From Rosenfeld RM, Brown L, Cannon CR, et al.; for the American Academy of Otolaryngology – Head and Neck Surgery Foundation. Clinical practice guideline: acute otitis externa. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2006;134:S4–S23.
